prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how technology and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: B037 now ranks first for me. It joins a conceptual account of technology (the task approach) to transparent quasi-experimental evidence on import competition, and it changed both academic practice and the public debate on globalisation and automation. The China-shock papers date from 2013 and the task work is older, so replication and debate over magnitudes have had time to develop and the core finding of concentrated local adjustment costs has held up. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the identifiable authors of the trade-shock evidence, and Autor also carries the task and polarisation strand. That gives a prize with a clear, coherent credit structure and a general lesson about adjustment costs that matters well beyond labour economics.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. The task framework draws on authors outside the credited set, and recognition of Acemoglu (2024) and Goldin (2023) already covers part of the technology and skill-premium ground. Dropping Katz to avoid that overlap leaves out a central figure in the education-technology race and the skill-premium literature. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the robustness of shift-share designs, are still contested. The two strands, tasks and trade shocks, may also be judged separable contributions rather than one discovery.

responses.point: Friberg ranked B037 sixth and proposed Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He sees the China-shock strand as cleanly attributed to Autor-Dorn-Hanson, the technology strand as more diffuse, and the long-run interpretation as still contested.
responses.response: I agree that the trade-shock strand has the cleaner credit structure, and I have moved to his trio instead of my opening Katz variant. I disagree that the technology strand should therefore be dropped from the citation. Autor is central to the task and polarisation evidence, so it can be credited through him without naming further people. I accept that persistence of the effects is still debated, which is why the citation stresses empirical analysis of adjustment rather than settled welfare conclusions.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranked B037 first. She sees the choice between Dorn and Katz as forced by the three-name cap, notes that Katz's contribution partly overlaps with work by prior laureates, and observes that Acemoglu shaped the task framework and is not on the list.
responses.response: I share her reading of the overlap and it is the main reason I now prefer Dorn to Katz. Katz's skill-premium work sits close to ground already recognised in 2023 and 2024, whereas Dorn is a co-author of the import-shock papers, which are the least-overlapping empirical contribution. I concede the cost: this choice leaves out the long-run education-versus-technology framing, and the committee should weigh that openly rather than treat it as settled. I would also not claim the task framework as a discovery of this trio alone.

responses.point: Boppart ranked B001 first and B037 second. He treats Obstfeld and Rogoff as the clear two architects of a framework that has been absorbed into central-bank modelling, and he sees B037 credit as spread across authors, including uncredited Levy-Murnane and Acemoglu.
responses.response: His attribution point against B037 is fair, and I keep B001 as my first alternative because its two-name credit is cleaner. Where I differ is on what each prize rewards. B001 is mostly a framework and synthesis, and the disconnect puzzles remain unresolved, so the claim to a confirmed discovery is weaker. B037 offers design-based evidence that has been replicated and tested, with the caveat on magnitudes. I would not call his ordering wrong. I rank the two differently on confirmation, not on importance.

responses.point: Stromberg ranked B045 first as a unified theory-plus-evidence programme on constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity. He acknowledges that the 2024 institutions prize may reduce appetite for a second institutions-themed award.
responses.response: I ranked B045 second in my opening and still regard it as a coherent and mature field-defining programme. On reflection, the 2024 overlap and the weaker causal identification in the cross-country constitutional evidence, which he and Teorell both note, make it a riskier lead than B037. I would not place it above a candidate with better-tested identification. I also note that B045 is close to my own field of dynamic political economy, so I discount my confidence in ranking it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the task/technology strand and the China-shock strand as one discovery or two.
Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name; my choice rests on overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes, not on a clear difference in merit.
How persistent and how large the China-shock effects were, and how robust shift-share identification is.

My first-ranked B004 stays a strong alternative on attribution (a jointly authored pair), but mixed empirical support for protection-for-sale and Helpman's split credit with B008 leave it a weaker lead; I rely on my own recollection of the literature and have not verified sources independently.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-triggering connection to the credited names of B037 is apparent from the supplied profile. I co-authored with committee colleagues Boppart and Friberg, and frequently with Krusell (the secretary); none of these is a candidate. My research areas (macroeconomics, dynamic political economy, social mobility) are near B045, B013 and B038, and I have discounted my confidence in ranking those. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
